introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0580 Physics 1, GCE Ordinary Level, June 2021, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; decide which answer is appropriate. Section 1 (questions 1 to 42) has independent questions; Section 2 (questions 43 to 50) has two practical situations, each followed by a set of questions (questions 43-46 and 47-50). Calculators are allowed.

**Constants:** acceleration of free fall $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; speed of light in vacuum $c = 3\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; charge on an electron $e = 1.6\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following values below represents momentum?
questions.corrige_markdown: Momentum is mass times velocity, $p = mv$, so its unit is $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The other units belong to other quantities: the newton is the unit of force, the pascal the unit of pressure, and $\mathrm{N\,m}$ is the unit of work (or of the moment of a force). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The base unit of length is the:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the SI system the base unit of length is the metre. The millimetre, centimetre and kilometre are multiples or sub-multiples of the metre, not the base unit. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following pairs are all scalar quantities?
questions.corrige_markdown: A scalar has magnitude only. Work (energy transferred) and time are both scalars. In the other pairs one quantity has a direction: momentum (B), displacement (C), and velocity and force (D) are vectors. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the graphs in figure 1 best represents the relationship between the acceleration of a moving car and its mass, when the force acting on the car is constant?

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Options as printed (graphs of $a$ against $m$):* A) a decreasing inverse-type curve that starts a little away from the $a$-axis and flattens towards the $m$-axis; B) a decreasing inverse-type curve that starts on the $a$-axis and flattens towards the $m$-axis; C) a straight line sloping downwards that cuts the $m$-axis; D) a straight line through the origin sloping upwards.
questions.corrige_markdown:
By Newton's second law, $F = ma$, so for a constant force $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$: acceleration is **inversely proportional** to mass. The graph of $a$ against $m$ must therefore be a hyperbola-type curve that falls steeply for small masses and flattens out for large masses, without ever reaching zero.

Graph C (a straight line that reaches $a = 0$ at a finite mass) and graph D ($a$ proportional to $m$) are wrong. Graphs A and B both show the inverse-type curve; B is the one that hugs both axes like the ideal curve $a = F/m$, while A has the same shape but starts away from the $a$-axis. Because the printed options A and B cannot be told apart reliably, no single letter is designated here.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these units is equivalent to joule per coulomb ($\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$)?
questions.corrige_markdown: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$, so $1\,\mathrm{V} = 1\,\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$. The watt is $\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$, the ampere is $\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$ and the ohm is $\mathrm{V\,A^{-1}}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For a body to stay in equilibrium:
questions.corrige_markdown: A body is in equilibrium when it neither accelerates nor rotates. That needs both conditions: the resultant force is zero (no translation) and the resultant moment is zero (no rotation). Option A alone allows a spinning body, and option C only deals with vertical forces. Option D is meaningless because a force and a moment cannot be compared. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the net force must be zero
the net force and the sum of the moments must be zero
the upward forces must be equal to the sum of the downward forces
the net force must be greater than the sum of moments.

questions.enonce_markdown: In a velocity-time graph the area between the graph and the time axis gives:
questions.corrige_markdown: Distance is velocity multiplied by time, so the area under a velocity-time graph (height $v$ times width $t$) is the distance travelled. The gradient of the graph, not its area, gives the acceleration. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Seat belts reduce injury on users in the case of accidents by:
questions.corrige_markdown: The force that stops the passenger is $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$. For the same change of momentum, a seat belt stretches slightly and so makes the stopping time longer; a longer time means a smaller stopping force. Options A, B and C contradict this relation. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: reducing the stopping time and increasing the stopping force
increasing the stopping time and increasing the stopping force
reducing the stopping time and reducing the stopping force
increasing the stopping time and reducing the stopping force

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these energy resources is non-renewable?
questions.corrige_markdown: Petroleum took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced on a human time scale, so it is non-renewable. Biomass, tidal energy and solar energy are renewed continuously. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following pairs of forces are both non-contact forces?
questions.corrige_markdown: A non-contact force acts without the bodies touching: gravitational (weight), magnetic and electrostatic forces. Upthrust, air resistance and friction all need contact with a fluid or a surface. Only option D has two non-contact forces. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Air resistance force and electrostatic force

questions.enonce_markdown: A ball of mass $0.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has kinetic energy of:
questions.corrige_markdown: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 0.5\,\mathrm{kg}\times(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2 = 0.25\times 100 = 25\,\mathrm{J}$. Forgetting to square the velocity gives $2.5\,\mathrm{J}$, and forgetting the factor $\tfrac12$ gives $50\,\mathrm{J}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What type of energy is stored in a compressed spring?
questions.corrige_markdown: Work done to compress the spring is stored in the deformed spring as elastic (strain) potential energy, and is released when the spring expands. The spring is not moving (not kinetic) and its height has not changed (not gravitational). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The density of a substance is the:
questions.corrige_markdown: Density is $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$, the mass contained in one unit of volume. A and B give a fixed mass, not a density, and C is the inverse quantity (volume per unit mass). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: volume of a unit mass of the substance
mass of a unit volume of the substance

questions.enonce_markdown:
In figure 3 an irregular-shaped object is put into a measuring cylinder containing water.

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

The volume of the object is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The object displaces its own volume of water. The water level rises from $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ to $145\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, so $V = 145 - 100 = 45\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. The reading $145\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ (option C) is the final level of water plus object, not the volume of the object. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The hydraulic jack works on the principle that the:
questions.corrige_markdown: This is Pascal's principle: a pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished and equally to every part of the liquid. Because the pressure is the same on the small and large pistons, $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$, a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston. It is the pressure, not the force, that is transmitted equally. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: force applied to a liquid is transmitted equally to every part of the liquid
force applied to a liquid is transmitted in proportion to the area of contact
pressure applied to a liquid is transmitted equally to every part of the liquid
pressure applied to a liquid is transmitted in proportion to the area of contact

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the pressure, in pascals, in a liquid of density $1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, at a depth of $10\,\mathrm{m}$?
questions.corrige_markdown: $p = \rho g h = 1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\times 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\times 10\,\mathrm{m} = 100\,000\,\mathrm{Pa} = 10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ (using $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and taking the pressure due to the liquid alone). Using $h = 1$ or forgetting a factor of 10 gives $10^{4}$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the graphs in figure 4 shows how the pressure at a given depth varies with the depth of the liquid?

![fig-3](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $p = \rho g d$ with $\rho$ and $g$ constant, pressure is directly proportional to depth: the graph of $p$ against $d$ is a straight line through the origin sloping upwards (graph A). B slopes down, C is constant and D is a flattening curve, none of which is proportionality. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When evaporation takes place the temperature of the remaining liquid drops because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Only the most energetic (fastest) molecules have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attraction of the others and leave the surface. The molecules left behind have a lower average kinetic energy, which means a lower temperature. A is the opposite of what happens. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the pressure on the liquid is decreasing
the pressure on the liquid is increasing

questions.enonce_markdown: Absolute zero ($0\,\mathrm{K}$) is the same as a Celsius temperature of:
questions.corrige_markdown: $T(^\circ\mathrm{C}) = T(\mathrm{K}) - 273$, so $0\,\mathrm{K} = -273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The value $273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (option D) has the wrong sign, and $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is the melting point of ice ($273\,\mathrm{K}$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Water is used in car radiators because it has a:
questions.corrige_markdown: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it can absorb a large quantity of heat from the engine for a small rise in temperature and then carry that heat to the radiator to be lost to the air. This is the property that makes it a good coolant. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: During the night the temperature of the sea water is higher than that of the sandy sea shore. This is because sea water:
questions.corrige_markdown: Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than sand. For the same heat loss at night the sea water cools down very little, while the sand, with its lower heat capacity, cools quickly. Option D states the opposite, and option A concerns heating during the day, not the slow cooling at night. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: is a better absorber of heat than sand
is a poorer radiator of heat than sand
has a higher heat capacity than sand
has a lower heat capacity than sand

questions.enonce_markdown:
The specific latent heat of fusion of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to convert:

*Options as printed:* A) $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of the substance from solid to liquid at constant temperature; B) $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of the substance from liquid to gas at constant temperature; C) a unit mass of the substance from solid to liquid at constant temperature; D) a unit mass of the substance from liquid to gas at constant temperature.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The specific latent heat of fusion is the quantity of heat needed to change **unit mass** (that is, $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ in SI units) of a substance from solid to liquid **at its melting point, without any change of temperature**. Its unit is $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

Options B and D describe the change from liquid to gas, which is vaporisation, so they are wrong. Options A and C both state the correct definition in different words ("$1\,\mathrm{kg}$" and "a unit mass" mean the same thing), so the printed question has two correct options and no single letter is designated here.

questions.enonce_markdown: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by:
questions.corrige_markdown: Between the Sun and the Earth there is empty space (a vacuum). Conduction and convection need a material medium, so heat can only cross this space as infrared and other electromagnetic radiation. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When measuring the specific heat capacity of liquids the calorimeter and its contents is lagged so as to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Lagging is a poor conductor of heat. It reduces the heat lost to (or gained from) the surroundings, so nearly all the heat supplied goes into the liquid and the result for the specific heat capacity is more accurate. Stirring, not lagging, ensures even distribution of heat, and lagging has nothing to do with electrical contact. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A car is moving with uniform acceleration. Its velocity-time graph is:

![fig-4](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Uniform (constant) acceleration means the velocity increases by equal amounts in equal times, so the graph of $v$ against $t$ is a straight line sloping upwards (graph B). Graph A is a constant velocity (zero acceleration), and C and D are curves, which means the acceleration is changing. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Dust particles often stick on television screens because the:
questions.corrige_markdown: The screen of a television becomes electrostatically charged while it is working. A charged object attracts neutral (uncharged) dust particles by induction: the charge on the screen pulls the opposite charge in the dust towards it, so the attraction is stronger than the repulsion and the dust sticks. Option B reverses the roles, and option D is wrong because an uncharged screen would not attract the dust. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: television screens become charged and so attract the oppositely charged dust particles
dust particles become charged and so attract the uncharged television screens
television screens become charged and so attract the uncharged dust particles
television screens, whether charged or not, attract dust particles

questions.enonce_markdown: Electrical power is transmitted at high voltage in thick copper cables:
questions.corrige_markdown: The power lost in the cable is $P = I^2R$. For a given power $P = VI$, a high transmission voltage means a small current, and thick copper cables have a small resistance $R$. Both choices make the power loss as low as possible. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: so as to discourage people from stealing the cables along the way
so as to maintain a high voltage up to the consumer end
so as to keep power loss along the cable as low as possible
because transformers will step down the voltage to any level at the consumer end

questions.enonce_markdown: The effective voltage of electrical energy supplied to our homes by ENEO is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The domestic mains supply in Cameroon is rated $220\,\mathrm{V}$ (effective, or r.m.s., value). The peak value is larger, $220\sqrt{2}\approx 311\,\mathrm{V}$, so the $340\,\mathrm{V}$ of option D is not the effective voltage. $110\,\mathrm{V}$ is the mains voltage used in some other countries. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When we pay electricity bills, what are we paying for?
questions.corrige_markdown: The bill is calculated from the energy used, measured in kilowatt-hours: $E = Pt$. Power is only the rate of use of energy, and voltage is not \"consumed\". **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A voltmeter is connected in a circuit as shown in figure 5.

![fig-5](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

The voltmeter is connected as such because it has a very:
questions.corrige_markdown: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component whose potential difference is measured. It must have a very high resistance so that it draws very little current and does not change the current or the voltage in the circuit. A low resistance (A, C) would take a large current from the circuit, and a high resistance cannot draw a high current (B). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: low resistance and so draws low current
high resistance and so draws high current
low resistance and so draws high current
high resistance and so draws low current

questions.enonce_markdown:
The bar magnet in figure 6 is moved quickly towards the solenoid

![fig-6](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

The rule that can be used to determine the magnitude of the induced EMF generated in the solenoid is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Faraday's law says that the magnitude of the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage (a faster magnet gives a larger EMF). Lenz's law only gives the direction of the induced current, Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on a current in a field (motor effect), and the right-hand grip rule gives the direction of the field of a current. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In drawing of magnetic field lines, the stronger the field is the:
questions.corrige_markdown: The strength of a magnetic field is shown by how crowded the field lines are: where the field is strong the lines are drawn close together, where it is weak they are far apart. Parallel lines (A) show a uniform field, not a strong one. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: more parallel the field lines are
farther apart the field lines are
closer together the field lines are
more divergent the field lines are

questions.enonce_markdown: An optical pin is placed between the principal focus and the optical centre of a converging lens. The image formed is:
questions.corrige_markdown: When an object is closer to a converging lens than its principal focus, the refracted rays diverge. They appear to come from a point behind the object, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified, as with a magnifying glass. A real image forms only when the object is beyond the focus. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: real and bigger than the object
virtual and bigger than the object
real and smaller than the object
virtual and smaller than the object

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the diagrams in figure 7 best shows total internal reflection?

![fig-7](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Total internal reflection happens when a ray travelling inside the denser medium (glass) meets the glass-air boundary at an angle larger than the critical angle and is reflected back into the glass. Only diagram B shows this. Diagram A shows partial reflection of a ray in air at the glass surface, C shows a ray refracted out of the glass, and D shows a ray passing straight through. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Soft iron is used as the core of electromagnet because it is:
questions.corrige_markdown: An electromagnet must switch on and off quickly: the core has to become strongly magnetic when the current flows and lose its magnetism when the current stops. Soft iron is easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise. A material that is difficult to demagnetise (steel) would remain a permanent magnet. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: difficult to magnetise but easy to demagnetise
difficult to magnetise and difficult to demagnetise
easy to magnetise but difficult to demagnetise
easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is best suited for making the core of a transformer?
questions.corrige_markdown: The core of a transformer must carry a changing magnetic flux from the primary to the secondary coil, so it must be easy to magnetise and demagnetise at each cycle of the a.c. Soft iron does that. Copper and aluminium are not magnetic, and steel keeps its magnetism, which would waste energy. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A bar magnet with known poles is used to study the properties of a bar AB. If the south pole of the bar magnet attracts end A and also attracts end B of the bar, then the:
questions.corrige_markdown: Attraction alone does not prove that AB is a magnet: a magnet attracts any magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel). Only repulsion proves that a bar is a magnet. Here a south pole attracts both ends, so AB is a magnetic material; if it were a magnet, one of its ends would repel the south pole. A non-magnetic material is not attracted at all. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: north pole of the magnet will repel both ends of the bar AB
bar AB is a magnetic material
bar AB is a non-magnetic material

questions.enonce_markdown: The core of transformers are usually laminated in order to minimize heat loss due to:
questions.corrige_markdown: A changing flux induces circulating currents (eddy currents) in the iron core itself, which heat it. Building the core from thin sheets insulated from each other cuts these currents. Heat loss in the copper windings is due to their resistance (B), which lamination does not reduce. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tracks produced by alpha particles in a cloud chamber are:
questions.corrige_markdown: Alpha particles are heavy and strongly ionising: they lose their energy over a short distance (a few centimetres in air) and produce many ions along the way. Their tracks are therefore straight, short and thick. Beta particles, which are light, leave thinner and longer tracks that are often wavy, and gamma rays leave almost no track. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which symbol represents an alpha particle?

*Options as printed:* A) ${}^{4}_{2}\alpha^{2+}$; B) ${}^{4}_{2}\alpha$; C) ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$; D) ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{2-}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, nucleon number 4, proton number 2 and a charge of $+2$. It is written ${}^{4}_{2}\alpha$ or ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{2+}$.

Option D has the wrong charge sign ($2-$ would be a helium atom with two extra electrons). Options A, B and C are all used in textbooks for an alpha particle (A writes the charge explicitly, B is the usual symbol, and C is the helium nucleus written without its charge), so the printed question has no single clear key and no letter is designated here.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Alpha ($\alpha$), beta ($\beta$), and gamma ($\gamma$) radiations emitted from a source are deflected by a magnetic field pointing out of the page. The correct diagram of the outcome is:

![fig-8](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Gamma rays are uncharged, so they go straight on in every diagram. For a magnetic field out of the page and particles moving to the right, Fleming's left-hand rule (or $\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B$) shows that a positive particle is pushed down the page and a negative particle up the page. Alpha particles are positive, so they bend downwards; beta particles are negative, so they bend upwards. Beta particles, being much lighter, bend more sharply than alpha particles. Only diagram A has $\beta$ up and strongly curved, $\gamma$ straight and $\alpha$ down and less curved. B has $\alpha$ up, C has $\alpha$ undeflected and D has $\gamma$ deflected. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When trivalent atoms are added to a semiconductor, its conductivity increases. This process is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Adding a small amount of impurity atoms (here trivalent atoms such as boron or aluminium, which give a p-type semiconductor) to a pure semiconductor is called doping. Transmutation is the change of one element into another in nuclear reactions, rectification is turning a.c. into d.c., and transformation is the change of an a.c. voltage by a transformer. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 9 is part of a setup used to study the behaviour of waves in air.

![fig-9](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

The end X of the tube from the jar is connected to a:
questions.corrige_markdown: The figure shows an electric bell ringing inside a bell jar. To find out whether sound needs air, the air is gradually removed from the jar through the tube at X, which must therefore be connected to a vacuum pump. A barometer, manometer and Bourdon gauge only measure pressure; they do not remove air. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 9 is part of a setup used to study the behaviour of waves in air.

![fig-9](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

The substance applied at Y helps to:
questions.corrige_markdown: Y is the joint between the rim of the jar and the base plate. A substance such as grease or vaseline is applied there to seal the gap, so that air cannot leak back into the jar when the pump is working. The aim is not to change friction or to raise the air pressure. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: reduce static friction at the base
increase pressure of air at the base
increase static friction at the base
reduce the passage of air at the base

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 9 is part of a setup used to study the behaviour of waves in air.

![fig-9](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

When the instrument connected at point X is operating:
questions.corrige_markdown: The vacuum pump removes air from the jar. With less and less air to carry the vibrations, the sound heard from the bell becomes fainter. The bell itself keeps vibrating at the same rate (it can still be seen ringing), so C and D are wrong. B is the opposite of what happens. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the loudness of the sound from the electric bell gradually decreases
the loudness of the sound from the electric bell gradually increases
the vibration of the electric bell gradually decreases
the vibration of the electric bell gradually increases

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 9 is part of a setup used to study the behaviour of waves in air.

![fig-9](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)

This experiment shows that:
questions.corrige_markdown: As the air is pumped out the sound dies away, although the bell is still working, so sound needs a material medium such as air and cannot travel through a vacuum. The experiment is about sound, not light. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Light can travel in air but not in a vacuum
Light can travel in a vacuum but not in air
Sound can travel in air but not in a vacuum
Sound can travel in a vacuum but not in air

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 10 shows an electromagnet designed to pick up some metallic objects and released elsewhere.

![fig-10](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

A suitable material for the core X is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The core must be easy to magnetise and demagnetise, so that the objects are released when the current is switched off. Soft iron does this. Copper and wood are not magnetic, and steel would stay magnetised. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 10 shows an electromagnet designed to pick up some metallic objects and released elsewhere.

![fig-10](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

When the switch is closed the poles at the ends P and Q are respectively:
questions.corrige_markdown: The two ends of one electromagnet always have opposite poles, so N - N (A) and S - S (B) are impossible. To choose between C and D: the longer plate of the battery symbol is the positive terminal, so the conventional current leaves the top of the battery, goes through the switch, enters the winding near P and flows down the coil to Q. In the figure the front turns of the winding slope upwards to the right, so the current in the front turns flows from right to left. Seen from end Q (looking up the coil), the current therefore goes round **anticlockwise**, and an end seen with anticlockwise current is a North pole. So Q is a North pole and P is a South pole: P - Q is S - N. **Answer: D.**

Figure 10 shows an electromagnet designed to pick up some metallic objects and released elsewhere.

![fig-10](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

One material that cannot be picked up by the electromagnet can be made of:
questions.corrige_markdown: An electromagnet attracts magnetic materials: iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. Silver is not magnetic, so it cannot be picked up. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 10 shows an electromagnet designed to pick up some metallic objects and released elsewhere.

![fig-10](gce-ol-physics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)

Which of the following modifications will cause the electromagnet to pick up heavier objects?
questions.corrige_markdown: The strength of an electromagnet increases with the current and with the number of turns per unit length of the coil. More cells in the battery give a larger current, hence a stronger magnetic field. Making the core or the coil longer with the same number of turns does not make the magnet stronger (a longer coil spreads the same turns over more length and weakens the field), and an a.c. source makes the field keep reversing, which does not improve the pull. **Answer: C.**

Increasing the length of the coil
Increasing the number of cells of the battery
Changing the dc source to ac
